title: Disarming Srebrenica: The Agreement That Satisfied No One
content:
On 17-18 April 1993, General Sefer Halilovic, commander of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and General Ratko Mladic, commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, signed a demilitarization agreement for the Srebrenica enclave. The agreement came in the immediate aftermath of the VRS offensive that had driven tens of thousands of displaced Bosniaks into a shrinking perimeter around the town and just days after UN Security Council Resolution 819 had declared Srebrenica a safe area. It was an arrangement shaped entirely by military coercion -- a deal struck not between equals but between a besieging army and defenders who had been brought to the point of collapse.

The terms required the ARBiH to surrender all weapons within the enclave to UNPROFOR, which would oversee the collection and storage of arms. In exchange, the VRS would observe a ceasefire around Srebrenica, and a Canadian battalion of UNPROFOR would deploy into the enclave to monitor compliance. The agreement was presented as a step toward stabilization, but its fundamental asymmetry was apparent from the outset. The ARBiH garrison inside Srebrenica was being asked to disarm while the VRS formations surrounding the enclave retained their full complement of heavy weapons, armor, and artillery.

Implementation was fraught on both sides. The ARBiH surrendered a quantity of weapons but concealed others, judging -- not unreasonably -- that complete disarmament would leave the civilian population entirely at the mercy of forces that had already demonstrated willingness to shell populated areas. The VRS, for its part, continued to restrict humanitarian convoys and maintained its military stranglehold on the enclave. Neither side treated the agreement as a genuine commitment to peace; both regarded it as a temporary expedient imposed by circumstances.

The ICTY Krstic Trial Judgment (IT-98-33-T) addressed the demilitarization agreement in the context of the events that followed two years later. The judgment established that the VRS leadership never accepted the safe area concept as a permanent arrangement, viewing the enclaves as obstacles to the achievement of the strategic goals adopted by the Republika Srpska Assembly in May 1992. The partial demilitarization of Srebrenica's defenders, combined with the inadequate UNPROFOR deployment, created a situation in which the enclave's survival depended on international political will rather than any capacity for self-defense.

The UN's own retrospective assessment in the Report of the Secretary-General on Srebrenica (A/54/549, 1999) was forthright about the agreement's consequences. The report acknowledged that demilitarization placed the enclave's population in a position of extreme vulnerability. The ARBiH forces that remained could neither defend the perimeter effectively nor sustain offensive operations to break the siege. Meanwhile, the UNPROFOR contingent was too small to enforce the agreement's terms against either party and lacked the mandate or the military capability to deter a determined VRS assault.

For the Bosnian government, the Srebrenica demilitarization represented one of the war's most agonizing compromises. Accepting disarmament meant trusting the international community to protect a population that the government's own army could no longer defend. The leadership in Sarajevo understood the risk but saw no viable alternative -- the enclave was militarily unsustainable without external intervention, and the political cost of losing Srebrenica outright was unacceptable.

The agreement's legacy is inseparable from what followed. The weapons that were surrendered were never returned. The UNPROFOR presence that was supposed to guarantee security proved wholly inadequate when tested. The demilitarization of Srebrenica did not prevent catastrophe; it removed one of the few remaining obstacles to it.
